They were stopped a few hundred metres from the Commission’s office and eventually sat in protest. The Election Commission, however, gave a different account. Later, Delhi Police informed the Commission that a delegation led by Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi wanted to submit a memorandum. The ECI said the delegation wanted to meet at Parliament House Annexe, whereas its protocol required such meetings to be held at the Commission’s premises. It offered to send a senior-most officer to receive the memorandum, but the MPs declined. The explanation may address the question of procedure. items.title: What TechLaw.Fest revealed about the ecosystem
items.summary: "AI slop is becoming a real problem." One GC said plainly that she was seeing AI-generated material coming from her own team, from business stakeholders and from external counsel. The concern went beyond accuracy. The ease of producing polished-looking work was beginning to raise questions about whether the thinking behind it was becoming weaker. The comment stayed with me because it captured where the legal AI conversation seems to be heading. Much of the early discussion around generative AI focused on capability, particularly what it could draft, summarise or automate. At the Singapore-based conference, now in its 11th edition, the more interesting conversations were about judgement, quality, adoption and where lawyers were choosing to draw the line. Across the conference, the same sense of maturity appeared in different ways. The expo floor: Maturity beyond the usual names The expo floor had the global names you would expect, alongside established document management providers and the newer wave of AI companies competing for legal budgets. What interested me most were companies from markets like Korea that are already significant at home but relatively unfamiliar internationally. Some of the products we saw had clearly been developed over years of working with lawyers, with use cases built around specific workflows rather than whichever technology happened to be receiving attention at the time. The depth of those products was hard to miss. Years of iteration, customer feedback and use in local markets had shaped both the design and the problems they chose to solve. Some newer entrants to legal tech could learn as much from studying these established products as they can from looking at the latest AI launch. The exhibition also went well beyond software. items.title: POCSO Act victim has to be mandatorily heard before granting anticipatory bail to accused: Allahabad High Court
items.summary: The Allahabad High Court recently held that an order granting anticipatory bail to accused under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act (POCSO Act) without issuing notice or affording an opportunity of hearing to the victim is void ab initio and suffers from a jurisdictional defect [Veer Singh v. State of U.P. and 2 Others]. Justice Vivek Kumar Singh observed that issuing notice and hearing the victim or informant is a mandatory statutory command under the POCSO Act read with Rules of the POCSO Rules, 2020. The Court was hearing a plea moved by a complainant seeking cancellation of anticipatory bail granted to two accused by the Special Judge (POCSO Act), Bulandshahar, in a case arising out of an FIR lodged in February 2023. The trial court had granted pre-arrest bail on January 17, 2026, without issuing notice to the victim or informant. The accused opposed the plea, arguing that bail once granted cannot be cancelled without allegations of post-bail misconduct, tampering with evidence or threatening witnesses. Justice Vivek Kumar Singh The High Court rejected the argument. It clarified the distinction between cancelling bail for supervening circumstances and setting it aside for patent procedural illegality. "When an order granting pre-arrest bail is passed in direct contravention of a mandatory statutory command and in violation of the principles of natural justice (audi alteram partem), such an order is void ab initio and suffers from a jurisdictional error. It is liable to be set aside on this ground alone irrespective of whether the accused has misused the liberty after the order," the Court held. Relying on the Supreme Court’s ruling in Jagjeet Singh v. Ashish Mishra , the Bench reaffirmed that a victim has an unbridled statutory right to participate in proceedings from the stage of investigation until trial, including bail hearings. Consequently, the Court set aside the bail order and remanded the matter to the trial court to decide the plea afresh after issuing proper notice and granting reasonable time to file objections. To prevent hardship, the Court granted the accused interim protection from coercive action for six weeks. It also directed the Registrar General of the High Court to circulate the judgment to all special POCSO courts across Uttar Pradesh. Advocate Kanchan Chaudhary appeared for the complainant. items.title: Want to change your name as per astrology, numerology? Here's what Karnataka High Court said
items.summary: The Karnataka High Court recently set aside a civil court's refusal to allow a minor girl to change her name, and allowed the name change opted by her and her family for astrological and numerical reasons. Justice Hanchate Sanjeevkumar added that every Indian has a civil right to be recognised by their name and that people can, therefore, approach civil courts for a name change. "Every person in society is necessarily to be recognized by his/her name. It is a civil right of every citizen in India to be recognized by his/her name. Therefore, for correction or change of name, filing a suit before the Civil Court is maintainable, as it relates to the adjudication of a civil right," the Court said. In this case, the Court also noted that changing the name change was not objected to by anyone, and that it would not cause any harm to any person. Justice Hanchate Sanjeevkumar Karnataka High Court It is a civil right of every citizen in India to be recognized by his/her name. Therefore, for correction or change of name, filing a suit before the Civil Court is maintainable The Court was dealing with a plea filed by a minor girl through her father. At birth, she was named 'Lakshmi'. However, her parents later sought to change her name to 'Veena' on the belief that this name would bring more prosperity. The girl, represented by her father (plaintiffs), therefore filed a civil suit seeking a declaration that her name is Veena. The civil court, however, dismissed the suit on the ground that there was no document to show her name should be corrected to 'Veena', nor did the parents first approach the school she was enrolled in to change her name. This ruling was challenged before the High Court. The plaintiffs pointed out that there was a circular issued by the government of Karnataka which stated that a civil court decree was a must for a name change. The plaintiffs also placed on record public notices issued in newspapers about the proposed name change. The High Court granted the plaintiffs relief. The Court pointed out that the trial court had erred when it insisted on documentary proof that the girl's name is Veena, since the suit was filed for a name change and not a name correction. " This reasoning of the Trial Court is unwarranted, as it is not the case of the plaintiff that, at the initial stage, while admitting the plaintiff to the school, her name was wrongly mentioned as 'Lakshmi N.' The plaintiff simply desires to be called as 'Veena N.' and not 'Lakshmi N.”

Singh added that the matter concerns the federal structure of the country. "There is urgency. Otherwise, it will really... The State is going into polls. It is a clear case concerning the federal structure, which is being violated. I am only saying there is some urgency. I would not have prayed otherwise," the senior counsel said. items.title: Andhra Cabinet adopts resolution congratulating PM Modi’s 25 years in public office
items.summary: The Andhra Pradesh Cabinet on October 7 adopted a resolution congratulating Prime Minister Narendra Modi on completing 25 continuous years in public office as the head of a government. Modi was sworn in as the Chief Minister of Gujarat on October 7, 2001, a post in which he continued till 2014, when he became the PM. Meanwhile, Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister Chandrababu Naidu is on a two-day visit to Delhi from October 7, where he is scheduled to meet PM Modi, Union Home Minister Amit Shah, Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, and other Union Ministers. The visit comes amid heightened protests by the Opposition, student outfits, and the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. CM Naidu plans to seek assistance from the Union government for various projects such as approval for the Visakhapatnam Metro Rail and Beach Corridor, and special financial assistance in view of the drought-like conditions due to the impact of El Niño. He is also expected to seek the Union government’s support to conduct the Godavari Pushkaralu river festival next year, and river-linking initiatives in the state. Addressing the media after the Cabinet meeting, Andhra Pradesh Information and Public Relations Minister Kolusu Parthasarathy spoke about the resolution marking PM Modi’s 25 years in office and said that the Chief Minister and all the Ministers present expressed their respect for PM Modi and “how he has brought reforms in governance, how he grew from the lowest level to the Prime Minister, and his discipline, integrity, commitment, and determination to take the country to great heights.” Parthasarathy also said that CM Naidu instructed all the Ministers not to limit the resolution to a document, but examine it carefully and consider “how to emulate PM Modi’s great traits, how we can evolve and take the state and our districts forward.” Congratulating PM Modi on the occasion in an X post, CM Naidu said India was “fortunate to have the right leader, at the right time, in the right place.” 25 years of public service is a remarkable milestone in the journey of Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi Ji. items.title: ‘Dress is a personal choice’: Kerala HC backs woman’s right to wear what she chooses
items.summary: The Kerala High Court has declared that a citizen’s choice of attire is a matter of personal choice and that nobody can dictate what a person should wear based on social customs or personal notions of what is appropriate. Justice PV Kunhikrishnan made the observation while disposing of a petition filed by Sindhu S Nair, Headmistress of Eeswara Vilasom High School, Kottarakkara, against Suresh Kumar, the school manager. Sindhu had alleged that the manager prevented her from entering the school because she was wearing a churidar instead of a saree. The court noted that the dispute, at first glance, appeared to concern a simple question of attire. However, it said the issue had a deeper constitutional and institutional significance as it involved “the dignity, autonomy and professional standing of an educated woman” and the limits of managerial authority over her personal choice of dress. According to Sindhu’s petition, Suresh entered her office on February 3, 2026 and allegedly told her that she should not wear a churidar to school. She further alleged that he called security personnel in her presence and instructed them not to allow her into the school if she came wearing a churidar. The following day, the petitioner was allegedly stopped at the school gate because she was wearing a churidar. She complained to the police, following which she was allowed to enter the school premises. An FIR was subsequently registered based on her complaint. Sindhu relied on a 2015 circular issued by the General Education Department, which, according to the court, permits teachers to wear churidars. The court stressed that the case was not a contest between a saree and a churidar. “The Constitution does not make a woman's dignity contingent on her conformity with another person’s preferred mode of attire,” Justice Kunhikrishnan observed. “Dress is a personal choice. No one can restrict it, and no one can dictate which dress an individual must wear,” the court said, adding that the dignity and cultural tradition attached to an attire should be decided by the person concerned, rather than society. The court further held that “no one can dictate that a person should wear a particular attire unless there is backing of law in connection with the dress code of an institution or other establishment.” Since the government circular permitted teachers to wear churidar, the court said Suresh Kumar could not interfere with the petitioner’s choice of attire. items.title: HD Kumaraswamy alleges DK Shivakumar used sting operation to oust Siddaramaiah
items.summary: Union Minister HD Kumaraswamy on Wednesday, October 7, alleged that Karnataka Chief Minister DK Shivakumar had conducted a “sting operation” against his predecessor Siddaramaiah and that the material was used to force him out of the post. Kumaraswamy made the allegation while reacting to Shivakumar’s reported warning to his Cabinet colleagues about possible sting operations targeting ministers. He claimed that Shivakumar was now using the threat to keep his ministers under control. “Congress leaders themselves have told me that Shivakumar became Chief Minister after carrying out a sting operation and submitting it to the high command,” Kumaraswamy told reporters at the Janata Dal (Secular) office in Bengaluru. He alleged that Siddaramaiah had been called to Delhi on the pretext of discussions on Cabinet expansion but was instead confronted with the alleged sting material and pressured to resign. Kumaraswamy claimed the Congress high command, Shivakumar, and a media organisation were involved. Kumaraswamy did not provide details of the alleged sting operation, including when it was conducted, what it purportedly recorded, or what material was allegedly used against Siddaramaiah. “Who conducted the sting, who was behind it, and which media organisation was involved are known to everyone,” he said. He also questioned Shivakumar’s warning to his ministers, asking whether the Chief Minister did not trust his Cabinet colleagues and whether this was how a state should be governed. Shivakumar had reportedly cautioned his ministers at a Cabinet meeting on October 6 to remain vigilant about possible sting operations. Deputy Chief Minister G Parameshwara and Municipalities Minister HC Balakrishna confirmed that the Chief Minister had raised the issue. Parameshwara said Shivakumar, who holds the Intelligence portfolio, had received information from the department and had therefore asked ministers to be careful. Balakrishna said the warning was about possible attempts by the Opposition to defame the government. According to media reports, Shivakumar also showed ministers a file containing details of alleged ongoing sting operations and a list of around five ministers who were purportedly being targeted. Kumaraswamy alleged that Shivakumar had previously used similar tactics against political rivals and referred to the controversies involving Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) leader Ramesh Jarkiholi and Congress leader KN Rajanna. items.title: ED arrests ex-KPSC chairman Sahukar, member Geetha in veterinary officer recruitment scam
items.summary: The Enforcement Directorate (ED) on Tuesday, October 6, arrested former Karnataka Public Service Commission (KPSC) chairman Shivashankarappa S Sahukar after raiding his home for the second time in connection with the KPSC scam. Shivashankarappa S Sahukar is being investigated for alleged irregularities in the recruitment of 400 veterinary officers. Sahukar had been a KPSC member since 2019 and was appointed chairman in 2021. He was recently suspended after the allegations came to light. The CID is investigating the irregularities separately, while a High Court order concerning a separate Special Investigation Team (SIT) has been challenged in the Supreme Court. KPSC member BV Geetha, who was also raided the same day, was arrested as well. Arrest procedures for both were completed on Tuesday. An ED team reached Sahukar's residence in Dollars Colony around noon. Sahukar was at home and was questioned while officials executed the search warrant. The agency had previously raided him on August 18. The KPSC, which fills vacancies in the state government, has been under scrutiny over the veterinary officers' exam held on January 8 and 9 this year. IAS officer Gyanendra Kumar Gangwar, 41, who served as the commission's Controller of Examinations from early 2024 to March 2026, is alleged to have worked with Basavaraj Kannale to solicit and collect bribes from candidates seeking to pass the exam and secure jobs. Gangwar has been suspended by the Karnataka government. Gangwar allegedly leaked the question paper along with answers to around 20 candidates, who paid between Rs 20 lakh and Rs 40 lakh each through Kannale. During the CID and ED investigations, Kannale, 36, allegedly told investigators that Gangwar received about Rs 1.30 crore of the Rs 1.52 crore collected from candidates. During custodial interrogation, Gangwar allegedly named Sahukar, Geetha and two other KPSC members, Shanta Hosmani and Elfreda D'Silva, saying they had approached him regarding certain candidates. Separately, LiveLaw reported that a Bengaluru court has granted an ex parte temporary injunction granted to Kannale restraining several media houses and social media platforms from publishing, telecasting or broadcasting unverified and sensationalised content. Kannale, who is Accused No. 6 in Crime No. 89/2026 registered at Vidhana Soudha Police Station, is also under investigation by the CID, the SIT and the ED. He is currently in judicial custody.

items.title: Madras HC questions claim that Vijay’s alleged asset non-disclosure can void his election
items.summary: The Madras High Court, on October 7, asked how alleged discrepancies in Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay’s election affidavit could amount to undue influence on voters or justify setting aside his victory from Perambur. Justice V Lakshminarayanan raised the questions while hearing Vijay’s plea seeking dismissal of an election petition challenging his victory in the April 2026 Assembly polls. The election petitioner, S Dinesh, has alleged discrepancies involving several properties in Vijay’s 2026 nomination affidavit. The judge asked the petitioner’s counsel how the alleged non-disclosure of assets worth around Rs 30 crore could have influenced voters when Vijay had declared assets worth more than Rs 600 crore. He also questioned whether a voter would have been swayed by differences of a few crores or lakhs in the declared value of properties. The judge further asked whether Vijay, a prominent film actor with several properties, could personally be expected to know every detail in his asset declaration, particularly if the affidavit had been prepared with the assistance of a chartered accountant. Justice Lakshminarayanan also questioned the allegation that the returning officer improperly accepted Vijay’s nomination. He asked how a returning officer could be expected to verify the correctness of the assets declared in the affidavit. The petitioner’s counsel, NC Ashok Kumar, argued that the returning officer’s role was limited to a summary inquiry and that questions about whether a declaration was knowingly false or deliberately made could only be established through evidence during the trial of an election petition. He relied on a 2009 judgment of Justice V Ramasubramanian in Krishnamoorthy versus Sivakumar, which held that incorrect, incomplete, false or withheld information could interfere with the free exercise of a voter’s electoral right. He said the judgment was affirmed by the Supreme Court in 2015. The counsel also cited the Supreme Court’s 2013 judgment in Resurgence India versus Election Commission of India, which held that a voter’s right to know about a candidate is an integral part of the freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution. After hearing the submissions, Justice Lakshminarayanan told senior counsel Gopal Sankaranarayanan, appearing for Vijay, that the petitioner’s reliance on the judgments had changed the complexion of the case and asked him to respond on October 8. items.title: ‘If Gyanesh Kumar doesn’t resign, PM Modi will have to go’: Telangana CM Revanth in Delhi
items.summary: Amid heightened protests against the Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over his handling of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, Telangana Chief Minister A Revanth Reddy went to New Delhi on October 7 to express solidarity with Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi. However, the Delhi police stopped him from joining their protest. Speaking to media outside the Barakhamba Road police station where Rahul Gandhi and other Congress leaders were detained, Revanth said that instead of arresting the people who have committed mistakes during the SIR, the police had detained Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi, Priyanka Gandhi and Mallikarjun Kharge. He said that Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation would eventually lead to Prime Minister Narendra Modi exiting the PM’s chair. “Narendra Modi is trying to murder democracy. This movement will not end here,” Revanth said. He said that the SIR was happening under the instructions of PM Modi through Gyanesh Kumar. “They are trying to remove the voting rights of people. They are creating two types of people in the country, one with voting rights and those without,” he said. Revanth said that the BJP-led Union government had previously misused the Enforcement Directorate (ED) and Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) for political gains by targeting opposition leaders, and now, they are using even the Election Commission of India (ECI). “From the police action against Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi, we can see the intolerance of Narendra Modi and [Union Home Minister] Amit Shah. Today, to escape the consequences of their mistakes, to save their posts, they are getting police to attack Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi and other leaders,” CM Revanth said, condemning the detention of Congress leaders amid the protests in Delhi. He added that if Gyanesh Kumar doesn’t resign, PM Modi himself would have to quit his post.

items.title: Karnataka seeks to contest Cauvery water allocation, cites changing hydrological conditions
items.summary: Karnataka has signalled to the Supreme Court that it may seek to reopen the Cauvery water-sharing allocation, citing “inequitable allocation” and “changed circumstances” caused by changing hydrological conditions. According to a report by The Hindu , the state made the submission on October 7, in its response to Tamil Nadu’s application over the backlog in Cauvery water releases. Karnataka said it reserved the right to seek a reconsideration of the allocation made by the Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal and modified by the Supreme Court in 2018. Karnataka’s 40-page response, filed by advocate Nishanth Patil and settled by senior advocate Mohan Katarki, referred to the legal principle of rebus sic stantibus, under which arrangements can be revisited when circumstances underlying them have substantially changed. “In view of the looming inequity, the state of Karnataka reserves its right to apply in the changed circumstances for reopening of the inequitable allocation in the Award of Tribunal read with judgment of the Supreme Court. The normal practice is that the water allocations are periodically revisited,” the response said. The report said Karnataka also cited the Union government’s position on the Indus Waters Treaty of 1960, which India has sought to modify on the ground of changed circumstances, as an example of water-sharing arrangements being revisited. Under the Cauvery Tribunal’s award, as modified by the Supreme Court in 2018, the basin’s annual flow was assessed at 740 tmc ft at 50% dependability at the Lower Coleroon Anicut. Karnataka was allocated 284.75 tmc ft, Tamil Nadu 404.25 tmc ft, Kerala 30 tmc ft and Puducherry 7 tmc ft. Another 10 tmc ft was earmarked for environmental flows and 4 tmc ft as inevitable wastage to the sea. The framework provides for proportionate sharing of distress when the annual yield falls below 740 tmc ft because of deficient rainfall. Karnataka, however, argued that there is no scientific formula for determining how distress should be shared between the states, the report added. The state said the 2026-27 water year had become a distress year following the failure of the southwest monsoon between June and September. It argued that the allocation fixed by the Tribunal and affirmed by the Supreme Court did not account for subsequent changes in hydrology caused by climate change, environmental degradation and shifting monsoon patterns. items.title: Kerala HC gives govt 2 weeks to notify new anti-ragging guidelines
items.summary: The Kerala High Court has directed the state government to notify the proposed Anti-Ragging and Student Welfare Guidelines (2026) within two weeks, while observing that amendments to the Kerala Prohibition of Ragging Act (1998) may be necessary to strengthen punishment for ragging. A Division Bench comprising Chief Justice Soumen Sen and Justice C Jayachandran issued the direction on October 6, while considering petitions filed by the Kerala State Legal Services Authority (KeLSA) and Shamsudeen. The court noted that the 1998 Act is yet to be amended following the preparation of the proposed guidelines by a committee constituted by the state government on July 20, 2026. KeLSA had suggested several changes to the proposed guidelines, including amendments relating to the scope of the provisions, enhancement of punishment and reclassification of ragging as a cognizable and non-bailable offence. One of the specific concerns raised by KeLSA related to the wording of clause 6 of the proposed guidelines, which currently uses the expression “within, or without, any educational institution”. KeLSA suggested that the phrase be replaced with “within or outside” to make its meaning clearer. The Advocate General agreed that the wording in clause 6 could be modified for clarity. However, he submitted that enhancement of punishment and making the offence cognizable and non-bailable could not be incorporated merely through the guidelines. According to the state, such changes would require an amendment to section 4 of the Kerala Prohibition of Ragging Act which could be considered when an Amendment Act is brought in. The court accepted this position and directed that the wording in clause 6 be changed before the guidelines are notified. “We are confident that the legislature, while finalising the Bill, shall take into consideration the issues raised by the KeLSA, which appear to be relevant,” the bench said. The court also made it clear that the proposed guidelines were to be notified with the revised wording, directing that the expression “within, or without, any educational institution” be replaced with “within or outside, any educational institution”. The state government has been given two weeks from the date of the order to notify the guidelines. The bench did not itself alter the punishment provisions of the existing law, noting that such changes would require legislative intervention. items.title: Veteran actor Nana Patekar dies at 75 after cardiac arrest in Goa
items.summary: Veteran actor Nana Patekar died at the age of 75 after suffering a cardiac arrest at his residence in Dona Paula, Goa on October 8. According to media reports, Nana was found unconscious at his home after suffering severe chest pain and was taken to Manipal Hospital. Doctors attempted to revive him for around 45 minutes, but he could not be revived and was declared dead at 5.20 am. A medico-legal case has been registered and a post-mortem examination will be conducted. His son, Malhar Patekar, was in Pune when he received the news and left for Goa, according to reports. Nana, whose real name was Vishwanath Patekar, was one of the most distinctive actors in Hindi and Marathi cinema. Known for his intense screen presence and powerful dialogue delivery, he often played complex characters that fell outside conventional hero and villain roles. Born on January 1, 1951, in Maharashtra, Nana began his film career with the 1978 film Gaman . He went on to establish himself with performances in films including Ankush , Pratighaat , Salaam Bombay! , Parinda , Prahaar: The Final Attack , Angaar , Tirangaa , Krantiveer and Agni Sakshi . His later work included Khamoshi: The Musical , Yeshwant , Ab Tak Chhappan , Apaharan and Raajneeti . He also became hugely popular with a wider audience as gangster Uday Shetty in Welcome (2007) and Welcome Back (2015). He has also acted in Tamil movies like director Bharathiraja’s Bommalattam and director Pa Ranjith’s Kaala alongside Rajinikanth. Nana won three National Film Awards during his career. He received the Best Supporting Actor award for Parinda in 1990 and Agni Sakshi in 1997, while his performance in Krantiveer earned him the Best Actor award in 1995. He was awarded the Padma Shri in 2013 for his contribution to cinema and the arts. He also worked as a director and singer. His directorial credits include Prahaar: The Final Attack , while he lent his voice to songs in films including Yeshwant , Wajood and Aanch . In the 2000s, Nana continued to take on varied roles, earning praise for films such as Shakti: The Power , Ab Tak Chhappan , Apaharan and Taxi No. 9211 . He later appeared in Natsamrat , for which he won the Filmfare Award for Best Actor in 2016. Nana continued acting until the final year of his life.
